chapter: Kenny Kirkland, Wynton's quintet and the jazz business
title: How Wynton led the early quintet
summary: The trumpet player is always the leader, but Wynton gave freedom and the band was collaborative.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: On Columbia…. First, when Wynton put this group together--you just helped us understand how that was done--was it a collective feeling there, or was it a top-down kind of organization, Wynton’s group originally?

It’s both. Because when you play with a trumpet player, the trumpet player is the top. There has never been a band where that has never been the case. Like I said earlier, Sidney Bechet has often tried to reverse that, and never to any great success. It’s the nature of the instrument. Trumpet on top, saxophone second, piano, bass, drums. And that’s just kind of what it is. But, there is always a collective feel, because all of the guys are going to bring what they have to the table. Wynton, he was a bit of a micromanager, but he wasn’t like “Here’s every note that you’re supposed to play.” It wasn’t like that. There was a lot of leeway and a lot of freedom to just do what you do.
